group.title: Careers and the workplace
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A person who formally asks for a job or a place.
examples: We had over 200 {applicants} for the job.
wrong: The applicant never asked for the job at all.

words.meaning: A short letter you send with your resume explaining why you want the job.
examples: Tailor your {cover letter} to each company.
wrong: A cover letter is the envelope a bill comes in.

words.meaning: To choose a small number of the best people from all who applied.
examples: Five candidates were {shortlisted} for interview.
wrong: They shortlisted every single applicant, all three hundred of them.

words.meaning: An extra benefit you get from your job, besides your pay.
examples: Free lunch is one of the {perks} of working here.
wrong: A perk is a fine you pay when you arrive late.

words.meaning: To stop employing workers because there is not enough work.
examples: The factory {laid off} 300 workers.
wrong: The company laid off staff by hiring hundreds more.

words.meaning: Losing your job because your employer no longer needs your position.
examples: Over fifty staff face {redundancy} this year.
wrong: Redundancy is a promotion to a better job.

words.meaning: Officially telling your employer that you are leaving your job.
examples: She handed in her {resignation} after ten years.
wrong: His resignation meant he would stay in the job forever.

words.meaning: To remove someone from their job.
examples: He was {dismissed} for stealing from the company.
wrong: She was dismissed and given a raise for her great work.

words.meaning: Time off work that a woman takes before and after having a baby.
examples: She’s on {maternity leave} until March.
wrong: Maternity leave is extra work a new mother must do at night.

words.meaning: A person or company that pays people to work for them.
examples: My {employer} pays for my training.
wrong: The employer is the person who works for a company and receives a salary.

words.meaning: A person whose job is to find people for companies to employ.
examples: A {recruiter} called me about a job in sales.
wrong: A recruiter’s job is to stop companies from finding new staff.

words.meaning: A student or young person who works for a short time to gain experience.
examples: The summer {intern} helped with the research.
wrong: An intern is the company’s most senior director.

words.meaning: Someone who is being taught the skills for a job.
examples: Each {trainee} works alongside an experienced nurse.
wrong: The trainee has years of experience and teaches the senior staff.

words.meaning: Working for different companies on separate jobs, not for one employer.
examples: She’s a {freelance} designer.
wrong: As a freelance writer, he works full-time for one company on a fixed contract.

words.meaning: Working for yourself and running your own business.
examples: Many plumbers are {self-employed}.
wrong: He’s self-employed and works for a large company that pays his salary.

words.meaning: Working well together with others to reach a shared goal.
examples: Winning the contract took real {teamwork}.
wrong: Teamwork means everyone works alone and never shares.

words.meaning: A meeting where a manager reviews how well an employee has been doing.
examples: My annual {appraisal} is next week.
wrong: An appraisal is a party for the company’s birthday.

words.meaning: The series of higher jobs you can move up through during your working life.
examples: She climbed the {career ladder} quickly.
wrong: The career ladder is the ladder window cleaners use.

words.meaning: Chances of success or of getting a better job in the future.
examples: The job has good {prospects} for promotion.
wrong: The job has excellent prospects, so there’s no chance of moving up.

words.meaning: The feeling that your job is safe and you will not lose it.
examples: Many people value {job security} more than a high salary.
wrong: With great job security, she worried every day about being fired.

words.meaning: To find a skilled person working elsewhere and offer them a job.
examples: She was {headhunted} by a rival firm.
wrong: They headhunted her by refusing to offer her any job.

words.meaning: Being completely exhausted by too much work or stress over a long time.
examples: Long hours led to {burnout}.
wrong: After a relaxing holiday, she had burnout from feeling so rested.

words.meaning: To tell your employer officially that you are going to leave your job.
examples: I’m going to {hand in my notice} tomorrow.
wrong: She handed in her notice because she wanted to stay in the job forever.

words.meaning: A written list of the duties and skills a job involves.
examples: Read the {job description} before applying.
wrong: The job description is the salary paid at the end of the month.

words.meaning: The good feeling you get from enjoying your work.
examples: Nurses often report high {job satisfaction}.
wrong: His job satisfaction is high because he hates every minute at work.

words.meaning: An increase in the money you are paid for your work.
examples: I asked my boss for a {raise}.
wrong: She got a raise, so her salary went down.

words.meaning: A formal message from a company saying it wants to give you a position.
examples: She accepted the {job offer} the same day.
wrong: He got a job offer, which meant the company had rejected him.

words.meaning: A person who works at the same place as you.
examples: My {coworkers} threw me a birthday party.
wrong: My coworker has never worked at my company.

words.meaning: The department of a company that deals with hiring and staff matters.
examples: Send the signed form to {human resources}.
wrong: Human resources is the department that fixes the computers.

words.meaning: A move into a completely different type of work.
examples: At forty, he made a {career change} from banking to teaching.
wrong: Her career change meant she kept doing exactly the same work.

words.meaning: Of a job: with normal office hours, from morning to late afternoon.
examples: He quit his {nine-to-five} job to travel.
wrong: Her nine-to-five job keeps her at work all night.

words.meaning: A job with low pay and no chance of moving up.
examples: He felt stuck in a {dead-end job}.
wrong: A dead-end job offers great chances for promotion.

words.meaning: Someone who works well with others in a group.
examples: We’re looking for a {team player} who shares ideas.
wrong: As a team player, he refuses to help anyone.

words.meaning: An unseen barrier that stops some groups, such as women, from reaching top jobs.
examples: She broke through the {glass ceiling} to become CEO.
wrong: The glass ceiling is a window in the roof of the office.

words.meaning: Time off work, usually paid, because you are ill.
examples: He’s been on {sick leave} since his operation.
wrong: Sick leave is extra time at work when you are feeling healthy.

words.meaning: Looking for a new position to work in.
examples: After graduating, she spent months {job hunting}.
wrong: Job hunting means relaxing at home because you never want to work again.

words.meaning: Time spent in a workplace, especially to learn about a job.
examples: The course includes two weeks of {work experience}.
wrong: Work experience is a degree you get without ever working.

words.meaning: The group of abilities that a person has.
examples: Her {skill set} includes design and coding.
wrong: A skill set is a box of tools you buy at a hardware store.

words.meaning: The way people at work compete for power and influence.
examples: She hates the {office politics} at her company.
wrong: Office politics is a class about government that staff take after work.

words.meaning: Having enough skill to do a job well.
examples: She’s a very {competent} manager.
wrong: He’s a competent pilot who can’t fly a plane.
